meta.title: The Agent Loop: Observe, Decide, Act, Update
meta.thesis: A tool-using agent is an LLM wrapped in a repeating cycle that perceives state, chooses an action, runs a tool, and folds the result back in until the goal is reached or it safely stops.

modules.sub: Starts the spine: the problem the cycle solves.

questions.prompt: Why can't a single LLM call complete a task that requires checking live data and then making a decision based on it?

options.text: LLMs are too slow to handle multiple steps.
A single call produces one output and stops — it can't act on a result and then decide again.
LLMs can't read tool outputs at all.
Single calls always time out on complex tasks.

questions.explanation: A single call ends after generating one response. It has no mechanism to receive a tool result, reason about it, and take another action. That's exactly what the loop adds.

questions.prompt: What is the correct order of the four steps in the agent loop?

options.text: Decide → Observe → Act → Update
Act → Observe → Update → Decide
Observe → Decide → Act → Update
Observe → Act → Decide → Update

questions.explanation: The agent first observes its current context, then decides what to do, then acts (e.g. calls a tool), then updates state with the result — before the next turn begins.

questions.prompt: In the research-agent example, why did the agent need three turns instead of one?

options.text: The LLM forgot the goal between turns.
Each search tool call could only return one piece of data, so two searches were needed before the final answer could be written.
The turn budget forced it to stop after each step.
The agent re-observed the same state each time.

questions.explanation: The agent needed Tokyo's population (turn 1), then New York's (turn 2), before it had everything required to write the comparison (turn 3). Each turn's update fed the next observe.

questions.prompt: In your own words, explain what the 'update' step does and why skipping it would break the loop.
questions.explanation: State is the agent's working memory. Without updating it, each turn starts blind — the loop can't make progress because it never accumulates new information.
questions.acceptableAnswer: The update step writes the tool result (or any new information) back into the agent's state so the next turn can see it. If it's skipped, the next observe step reads stale data and the agent may repeat the same action or lose track of what it already found.

questions.prompt: Which failure mode does a 'turn budget' directly prevent?

options.text: Context overflow
Goal drift
Infinite spin
Stale state

questions.explanation: A turn budget sets a hard limit on how many times the loop can repeat. Without it, an agent that never decides the goal is met will keep calling tools indefinitely.

spans.text: Most agent failures trace back to a broken Observe step, not bad reasoning.
Here are the four most common ways it goes wrong.
The agent reads a tool result from an earlier turn, but the real world has changed since then.
Example: a flight price cached two turns ago is now sold out.
Most LLMs have a context-window limit.
When the conversation grows too long, early messages get cut.
The agent loses the original goal or a key user constraint — and doesn't know it.
A tool call fails silently — it returns an empty response or an error the agent ignores.
The agent treats the gap as 'no data found' and moves on with an incomplete picture.
Context and state can contradict each other.
The user said 'budget under £900' (context), but the state shows the only available flight is £950.
If the agent doesn't surface this conflict, it will either book the wrong flight or loop forever.
an agent that repeats the same tool call more than once usually has a stale or missing state.

blocks.title: Check your understanding: Observe

questions.prompt: At the start of each turn, an agent observes three things. Which option lists all three correctly?

options.text: The goal, the context, and the state
The goal, the tool list, and the user's name
The context, the output, and the next action
The state, the prompt template, and the model version

questions.explanation: An agent observes its goal (the task), its context (conversation + background), and its state (results of actions already taken). Tool lists and prompt templates are infrastructure, not the observation itself.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between 'context' and 'state' for an agent?

options.text: Context is what the agent was told; state is what the agent has done and found out.
Context is the tool result; state is the user's original message.
They mean the same thing — both refer to the conversation history.
State is set by the user; context is set by the model.

questions.explanation: Context = what the agent was given (instructions, conversation, background). State = what the agent has discovered or produced during the current session. Mixing them up is a common source of confusion.

questions.prompt: An agent is booking a flight. On turn 3 it searches for flights again, even though it already did that on turn 1. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The agent's state was missing or stale, so it had no record of the earlier search.
The agent's goal changed between turns.
The LLM ran out of tokens and had to restart.
The tool returned too many results on turn 1.

questions.explanation: Repeating the same tool call is the classic symptom of a missing or stale state. The agent can't see what it already did, so it starts over.

questions.prompt: In your own words: what does it mean for an agent's observation to be 'stale', and why is it a problem?
questions.explanation: Staleness happens when time passes between when a tool result was recorded and when the agent reads it. The world changes; the state doesn't. Any decision built on that gap can be wrong.
questions.acceptableAnswer: Stale means the agent is reading an old result that no longer reflects the real world. It's a problem because the agent will make decisions based on outdated information — for example, booking a flight that is already sold out.

questions.prompt: Why does a truncated context window create a hidden risk — one the agent itself may not notice?
questions.explanation: This is non-obvious because the agent doesn't receive an error — it simply has less information. It can confidently make a decision that contradicts a constraint it can no longer see.
questions.acceptableAnswer: When the context window fills up, early messages are silently dropped. The agent loses the original goal or a key constraint but has no way to know something is missing. It continues reasoning as if it has the full picture.

modules.summary: The agent gathers what it knows: the goal, the running context, and results from earlier actions. Good observation is what every later decision depends on.

blocks.analogy: A tool call is like filling out a form at the pharmacy: you write the medicine name (the tool) and the dosage and patient details (the arguments).

blocks.title: The Decide step inside the agent loop
blocks.caption: Decide sits between Observe and Act. Every turn the LLM reasons and picks one path.

spans.text: "What's the weather in Paris right now?"
Let's walk through the Decide step together.
Step 1 — The LLM reads its context
The model sees the user's question and the list of available tools:
. It has no weather data yet.
"I don't know the current weather. I have a tool that fetches it. I should call that tool."
Step 3 — The LLM decides: call a tool
. The loop moves to the Act step.
Step 4 — One turn later: decide again
"I have the answer. No more tools needed."
It decides to give a final answer and the loop ends.

blocks.title: Worked example: 'What's the weather in Paris?'

spans.text: The Decide step has a few common failure modes.
Knowing them helps you spot problems quickly.
. The tool can't run without it and returns an error.
This is the most common failure.
Results may be stale or irrelevant.
The model keeps calling tools even after it has enough information.
This wastes turns and can hit the
It usually happens when the goal is vague.
The LLM invents a tool name that doesn't exist.
The system can't find it and the turn fails silently or crashes.
Always validate the tool name against the allowed list.

blocks.title: How the Decide step breaks in practice

spans.text: If you use an AI assistant to generate tool-calling code, check these four things before trusting it.

items.text: Is the tool name exactly right? Compare it to your tool definitions — one typo breaks the call.
Are all required arguments present? Check the tool's schema for required fields.
Does the stop condition exist? Confirm the code can produce a final answer, not just tool calls.
Is the turn budget enforced? Make sure there's a max-turns guard so the loop can't run forever.

blocks.useWhen: The agent still lacks information it needs to answer, or must take an action in an external system to make progress.
blocks.avoidWhen: The context already contains everything needed to answer the user's question — calling a tool at that point wastes a turn and can introduce errors.
blocks.ruleOfThumb: If you can answer from what's already in context, stop. If you can't, call the most specific tool available.

questions.prompt: At the Decide step, the LLM can choose one of two paths. Which pair is correct?

options.text: Call a tool, or give a final answer
Observe the context, or update the state
Loop back, or reset the goal
Call a tool, or call a different tool

questions.explanation: The Decide step has exactly two outcomes: produce a tool call (name + arguments) to get more information, or produce a final answer when the goal is met.

questions.prompt: A tool call is made up of which two parts?

options.text: A tool name and a set of arguments
A goal and a context window
A reasoning trace and a final answer
A turn number and a memory update

questions.explanation: Every tool call has a name (which tool to run) and arguments (the inputs that tool needs). Both must be correct for the call to succeed.

questions.prompt: The LLM calls get_weather() but leaves out the city argument. What kind of failure is this?

options.text: Missing-argument failure
Wrong-tool failure
Hallucinated tool name
Turn budget exceeded

questions.explanation: A missing-argument failure happens when the tool call is formed but a required input is absent. The tool cannot run without it.

questions.prompt: In your own words: why would an agent keep calling tools even after it has enough information to answer?
questions.explanation: A vague goal makes it hard for the model to judge when it's done. This is a non-obvious failure: the tool calls succeed individually, but the loop never reaches a final answer.
questions.acceptableAnswer: The goal is vague or the model doesn't recognise that the context already contains the answer, so it keeps reasoning that more information is needed — wasting turns and risking hitting the turn budget.

questions.prompt: Name one thing you should check when an AI assistant generates a tool call for you.
questions.explanation: AI-generated tool calls can look correct but have subtle errors — a wrong name, a missing argument, or no stop condition. Checking these before running saves debugging time.
questions.acceptableAnswer: Any one of: the tool name matches the allowed list exactly; all required arguments are present; a stop/final-answer path exists; a max-turns guard is in place.

spans.text: The Act step touches real systems, so its failures have real consequences. These are the most common — and most dangerous — things to watch for.

A tool that deletes a file, sends an email, or charges a card cannot be undone. If the agent calls it on a wrong assumption, the damage is immediate. Always require a confirmation step before any irreversible
Silent failures — the tool returns nothing useful
may return an empty result, a timeout, or a vague error. If the runtime passes that back as-is, the agent may treat silence as success and move on with a false belief.
The LLM sometimes produces a call with a missing required argument or the wrong data type. The external system rejects it, but the agent may retry in a loop rather than stopping.
If every attempt fails and there is no
or retry limit, the agent loops forever. Always set a maximum number of turns and a hard stop on repeated failed calls.
A tool can succeed technically but change hidden state.
For example, a read-only search API might log the query and trigger a billing event. Treat any external call as potentially side-effecting until you have confirmed otherwise.

blocks.title: How the Act step breaks in practice
blocks.analogy: A tool call gone wrong is like posting a letter to the wrong address — the sender thinks the job is done, but nothing actually happened, and no one knows until it's too late.

spans.text: When an AI writes the code that dispatches tool calls, check these things before you trust it:

items.text: Does it validate arguments before sending? (Missing fields should raise an error, not silently pass None.)
Does it handle a failed or empty response — not just the happy path?
Does it guard destructive calls (delete, send, charge) with a confirmation flag or human-in-the-loop step?
Does it add the result to context as a new observation, not discard it?
Does it respect a turn budget or retry limit to prevent infinite loops?

questions.prompt: After the LLM produces a tool call, which part of the system actually contacts the external system?

options.text: The LLM itself, using its internal knowledge.
The agent runtime, which dispatches the call on the LLM's behalf.
The user, who must manually trigger the API.
The context window, which stores and sends the call.

questions.explanation: The LLM only produces the tool call as text (a name and arguments). The surrounding runtime code reads that output and actually contacts the external system. This separation is why the LLM can 'use' tools without having network access itself.

questions.prompt: Why must the tool result come back as a new observation rather than being discarded?

options.text: So the runtime can log it for billing purposes.
Because the LLM needs it in context to reason about what to do next.
To satisfy the external system's API contract.
So the agent can skip the next turn if the result is good enough.

questions.explanation: The agent loop works by feeding each result back as an observation. Without that, the LLM has no new information — it would reason from stale context and likely repeat the same action or make a wrong decision.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is the BEST example of a destructive tool call that needs a confirmation step?

options.text: search_web(query='best pizza in Rome')
get_weather(city='Tokyo')
delete_file(path='/invoices/2025-final.pdf')
list_calendar_events(date='2026-07-11')

questions.explanation: Deleting a file is irreversible — once done, the data is gone. Read-only calls like search or get_weather have no lasting side effects. Any action that cannot be undone (delete, send, charge) should require explicit confirmation before the agent runs it.

questions.prompt: In your own words: what is a 'silent failure' in the Act step, and why is it dangerous?
questions.explanation: Silent failures are especially tricky because no exception is raised. The agent just receives nothing useful and may carry on as if the call worked. Good runtimes check for empty or error responses and surface them explicitly as failed observations.
questions.acceptableAnswer: A silent failure is when the external system returns an empty result, a timeout, or a vague error, and the agent treats it as a success. It is dangerous because the agent continues with a false belief — it thinks it has information it does not actually have, which can lead to wrong decisions or fabricated answers.

questions.prompt: Trace the path of a single tool call from the moment the LLM produces it to the moment the next turn begins. Name each stage in order.
questions.explanation: This five-stage path is the core of the Act step. Each stage has a clear owner: the LLM owns stage 1, the runtime owns stages 2 and 4, and the external system owns stage 3. Knowing who owns what helps you debug when something goes wrong.
questions.acceptableAnswer: 1. LLM produces the tool call (name + arguments). 2. Runtime reads the call and dispatches it to the external system. 3. External system executes and returns a result. 4. Runtime packages the result as a new observation and adds it to context. 5. The next turn begins with that observation available to the LLM.

blocks.title: How the update step breaks in practice

blocks.useWhen: Keep the full result in context when the raw text itself matters for the next step — e.g. a code snippet the agent must edit, a legal clause it must quote, or a short result (< ~200 tokens) that is cheap to keep.
blocks.avoidWhen: Avoid keeping the full result when it is long, repetitive, or only partially relevant. Summarize or extract key facts instead, and write the summary to context while optionally archiving the full result to long-term memory.
blocks.ruleOfThumb: If the agent needs the exact words, keep them. If it only needs the meaning, summarize. When in doubt, extract 3–5 key facts and discard the rest.

blocks.intro: Answer from memory. These questions map directly to what you just learned.
blocks.title: Check your understanding: Update

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the Update step in the agent loop?

options.text: To call an external tool and get a result.
To fold the tool result into the agent's context so the next turn starts with richer information.
To decide which tool to call next.
To check whether the agent's goal has been reached.

questions.explanation: The Update step writes the result back into the agent's context (and optionally long-term memory). Without it, each turn would start from scratch and the loop would not build on itself.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes the difference between short-term context and long-term memory?

options.text: Short-term context is stored in a database; long-term memory lives in the conversation window.
Short-term context is the active window the LLM reads each turn; long-term memory is an external store that survives across sessions.
They are the same thing — both refer to the conversation history.
Short-term context is faster but more accurate; long-term memory is slower and less reliable.

questions.explanation: Short-term context is the text window the model sees right now — limited in size. Long-term memory is an external store (database, vector store, etc.) that persists beyond a single session.

questions.prompt: An agent keeps appending full tool results to its context on every turn. After 10 turns, it starts ignoring its original goal. What failure mode is this?

options.text: Stale context — the result was never written back.
Silent memory-write failure — the database timed out.
Over-stuffed context — the window filled up and the oldest content (including the goal) was dropped.
Termination failure — the agent never stopped looping.

questions.explanation: When the context window fills up, the LLM silently drops the oldest content. If the original goal was written early, it gets pushed out — and the agent loses track of what it was trying to do.

questions.prompt: In your own words: when should you keep a tool result verbatim in context, and when should you summarize it instead?
questions.explanation: The rule of thumb is: if the agent needs the exact words, keep them; if it only needs the meaning, summarize. Summarizing protects the context window and keeps the agent focused.
questions.acceptableAnswer: Keep verbatim when the exact wording matters for the next step (e.g. code to edit, a clause to quote, or a short result). Summarize when the result is long or only partially relevant — extract the key facts and discard the rest to avoid over-stuffing the context window.

questions.prompt: A research agent calls a search tool, gets a result, but never writes it back to context or memory. What will most likely happen on the next turn?

options.text: The agent will complete the task correctly using its training knowledge.
The agent will observe the same empty state as before and may repeat the same tool call.
The agent will automatically summarize the result and store it.
The agent will stop and ask the user for the missing information.

questions.explanation: Without an update, the agent's state does not change. On the next turn it observes the same context it started with, so it is likely to reason the same way and repeat the tool call it already made — a classic stale-context loop.

modules.summary: The result updates the agent's context and memory so the next turn observes a richer state. This is the link that makes the loop a loop instead of a one-shot.
objectives: After this you'll be able to explain how a result becomes part of the next observation.
After this you'll be able to distinguish short-term context from longer-term memory.
After this you'll be able to recognize stale or over-stuffed context as a failure mode.

blocks.title: Quick recall: what happens in the Update step?

spans.text: ends with a three-way decision: repeat, finish, or stop for safety.
There are three main reasons an agent stops:

items.text: — the agent's answer satisfies the original
— the agent has used its maximum allowed number of
. This is a hard safety ceiling.
— the same tool keeps failing, or the agent is going in circles. Continuing would waste resources or cause harm.

spans.text: Without these checks, an agent could loop forever — burning money, hitting rate limits, or returning a wrong answer with false confidence.

blocks.analogy: An agent loop is like a chef tasting a dish repeatedly — they stop when it tastes right, when the kitchen closes, or when they've burned it three times and need to call it.

blocks.analogy: A turn budget is like a parking meter — no matter how much you want to stay, the time runs out and you must leave.

blocks.caption: After every Update, the agent runs three checks before looping again. The first check that fires ends the loop.

blocks.title: A research agent decides whether to keep going

blocks.useWhen: The agent has retrieved all needed information and the answer directly satisfies the stated goal — choose 'finish'.
blocks.avoidWhen: The last tool call failed, the answer contains claims not backed by retrieved content, or the turn budget is already exhausted without a real result — do not mark the goal as met.
blocks.ruleOfThumb: If you can't point to a retrieved fact for every claim in the answer, the goal is NOT met — stop safely and say so.

blocks.intro: You've reached the end of the agent loop spine. These questions cover the whole loop — and especially when and why it stops.
blocks.title: Module 6 knowledge check: Loop termination

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the three main reasons an agent loop stops?

options.text: The goal has been met.
The turn budget has been exhausted.
The LLM produced a very long answer.
Repeated tool failures triggered a safe stop.

questions.explanation: The three termination reasons are: goal met, turn budget hit, and safe stop after repeated failures. Answer length is not a termination condition — an agent can produce a short or long answer on any turn.

questions.prompt: An agent has a turn budget of 10. On turn 7, it meets its goal. What should happen?

options.text: The agent must use all 10 turns before stopping.
The agent stops immediately and returns the answer.
The agent waits until turn 10 to confirm the goal.
The agent resets the turn counter and starts over.

questions.explanation: The turn budget is a ceiling, not a target. As soon as the goal is met, the loop exits — there is no reason to use remaining turns.

questions.prompt: Why is 'unsupported final claims' listed as a failure mode for termination?

options.text: The agent stopped too late and wasted turns.
The agent stopped on time but its answer contains facts it never actually retrieved.
The agent called a tool that was not on the allowed list.
The agent's context window was too small.

questions.explanation: Termination only controls when the loop ends — it does not guarantee the answer is correct. An agent can stop within budget and still return fabricated claims if it never verified them with a tool call. This is why you must check that every claim maps to retrieved content.

questions.prompt: In your own words: what is a turn budget, and what problem does it solve?
questions.explanation: The key ideas are: (1) it is a hard ceiling on the number of turns, and (2) its purpose is to prevent infinite or runaway loops that waste resources or never return an answer.
questions.acceptableAnswer: A turn budget is a maximum number of turns the agent is allowed before it must stop. It prevents the agent from looping forever — for example, when it gets stuck calling the same tool repeatedly or oscillating between plans without finishing.

questions.prompt: An agent is researching a topic. It calls a search tool four times in a row and gets an error each time. The turn budget still has 6 turns left. Should it keep trying? What should it do instead?
questions.explanation: This tests the 'safe stop after repeated failures' termination reason. A remaining turn budget does not mean the agent must keep going — if a tool is consistently failing, the right move is to stop safely and be transparent with the user.
questions.acceptableAnswer: No — it should trigger a safe stop after repeated failures. Continuing to call the same failing tool wastes the remaining budget and will not produce a better result. The agent should stop, return whatever it found before the failures, and tell the user why it stopped.

modules.summary: An agent must decide each turn whether to repeat or finish: goal met, turn budget hit, or a safe stop after repeated failures. We revisit the whole loop while covering its failure modes.
objectives: After this you'll be able to list the main reasons an agent loop stops.
After this you'll be able to explain why a turn budget prevents infinite loops.
After this you'll be able to name failure modes like repeated failed calls and unsupported claims.
modules.decisionItForces: Repeat the loop, finish, or stop for safety?

act.label: Act
act.laymanDefinition: The step where the chosen tool call actually runs against an external system.

llm.label: LLM
llm.laymanDefinition: A model that predicts and generates text, used here as the brain that reasons and picks actions.

goal.label: Goal
goal.laymanDefinition: The task the agent is trying to complete, which guides every decision it makes.

tool.label: Tool
tool.laymanDefinition: An external capability the agent can call, such as a search, a calculator, or a database query.

turn.label: Turn
turn.laymanDefinition: One pass through the loop: observe, decide, act, and update before deciding whether to repeat.

agent.label: Agent
agent.laymanDefinition: A language model wired into a repeating loop so it can take actions and use tools, not just answer once.

state.label: State
state.laymanDefinition: Everything the agent currently knows and has done so far in the task.

decide.label: Decide
decide.laymanDefinition: The step where the LLM reasons over the observation and chooses a tool or a final answer.

memory.label: Memory
memory.laymanDefinition: Information the agent keeps across turns so it doesn't forget what it has learned or done.

update.label: Update
update.laymanDefinition: The step where the result is folded back into context and memory for the next turn.

context.label: Context
context.laymanDefinition: The running set of information the agent currently has in view, including goal and recent results.

observe.label: Observe
observe.laymanDefinition: The step where the agent reads the goal, current context, and results of past actions.

reasoning.label: Reasoning
reasoning.laymanDefinition: The model thinking through what to do next based on what it just observed.

tool_call.label: Tool call
tool_call.laymanDefinition: A request from the agent naming a specific tool plus the arguments to run it with.

agent_loop.label: Agent loop
agent_loop.laymanDefinition: The repeating cycle of observe, decide, act, and update that drives an agent until its goal is met or it stops.

termination.label: Termination
termination.laymanDefinition: How and when the loop stops: goal reached, turn budget hit, or a safe stop on failure.

turn_budget.label: Turn budget
turn_budget.laymanDefinition: A maximum number of loop passes allowed, used to prevent the agent running forever.

external_system.label: External system
external_system.laymanDefinition: Anything outside the model the agent talks to, like an API, file, or website.

function_calling.label: Function calling
function_calling.laymanDefinition: The mechanism that lets an LLM emit a structured request to invoke a named tool with arguments.

nodes.what: Explains why a repeating observe→decide→act→update loop is necessary for tool-using AI agents.
nodes.label: Why the loop exists
nodes.orient: Why a single LLM answer isn't enough, and how the four-step cycle drives an agent.
nodes.relevance: This is the foundation of everything else in the lesson — every later module (tools, state, memory, termination) is a deeper look at one part of this loop.
nodes.laymanExplanation: A chatbot is like a vending machine — one button, one result; an agent is like a sous chef who keeps tasting, adjusting, and tasting again until the dish is right.

nodes.what: The Observe step is how an agent assembles its goal, context, and state at the start of every turn before making any decision.
nodes.label: Observe the state
nodes.orient: How the agent reads the goal, current context, and results of past actions before deciding.
nodes.relevance: Every later step in the agent loop — deciding, acting, updating — depends entirely on what the agent observed here; a weak observation means every downstream decision is built on shaky ground.
nodes.laymanExplanation: It's like a chef glancing at the order ticket, the half-finished dish, and the clock before touching anything — without that glance, every move is a guess.

nodes.what: How the LLM reasons over its context and decides whether to call a tool or give a final answer.
nodes.label: Decide the next action
nodes.orient: How the LLM reasons over what it observed and picks a tool or final answer.
nodes.relevance: Every agent you build depends on this decision — get it wrong and the agent calls the wrong tool, stalls, or never stops.
nodes.laymanExplanation: The Decide step is like a chef checking the order ticket and the fridge, then choosing whether to grab an ingredient or plate the dish.

nodes.what: The Act step runs the chosen tool call against an external system and feeds the result back as the next observation.
nodes.label: Act with a tool
nodes.orient: How the chosen tool call runs against an external system and returns a result.
nodes.relevance: Understanding Act tells you exactly how your agent reaches out to real services — and what can go wrong when it does.
nodes.laymanExplanation: Act is like placing a phone order: the agent tells the runtime what to order, the runtime calls the restaurant, and the receipt that comes back tells the agent what happened next.

nodes.what: The Update step writes a tool result back into the agent's context and memory, making the loop build on itself turn by turn.
nodes.label: Update the context
nodes.orient: How the result is folded back into context and memory so the next turn is smarter.
nodes.relevance: Without this step your agent forgets what it just learned — mastering it is what turns a one-shot call into a genuinely useful multi-turn agent.
nodes.laymanExplanation: It's like a chef tasting a dish mid-cook and updating their recipe notes before the next step — the tasting changes what they do next.

nodes.what: This module explains the three ways an agent loop ends: goal met, turn budget exhausted, or a safe stop after repeated failures.
nodes.label: Know when to stop
nodes.orient: How the loop terminates: goal met, turn budget, or a safe stop on failure.
nodes.relevance: Without a clear stopping rule, any agent you build can loop forever, waste resources, or return fabricated answers — this module gives you the checks that prevent that.
nodes.laymanExplanation: Knowing when to stop is like knowing when a recipe is done: you taste it (check the goal), watch the clock (turn budget), or accept it's burned and serve what you have (safe stop).

mentalMap.title: The Agent Loop — the map
mentalMap.oneLineThesis: A tool-using agent is an LLM wrapped in a repeating cycle that perceives state, chooses an action, runs a tool, and folds the result back in until the goal is reached or it safely stops.

buildOrder.label: Frame why an agent needs a loop instead of one answer
Observe: read the goal, context, and past results
Decide: reason and pick a tool or a final answer
Act: run the tool call against an external system
Update: fold the result into context and memory
Terminate: stop when the goal is met, budget is hit, or failure repeats
